1.pericope_label: Behold, I am against thee, and will draw forth my sword out of his sheath, and will cut off from thee the righteous and the wicked
debates: Whether the righteous suffer with the wicked in kind or only in appearance
What it means that the sword shall not return any more
Why the parable of the preceding chapter is restated plainly
outliers: Henry insists the graces and comforts of God make a great distinction where his providence seems to make none
Clarke argues that had none but the wicked been carried away their case would have been hopeless, with none left to preach repentance or reprove sin
Ellicott sets this sword against earlier judgments arrested in mercy, the scabbard taken back while the work was incomplete
Wesley states plainly that the righteous are commonly involved with others in public calamities
themes: Zion battered with her own artillery
No man ever complaining of getting to heaven too soon
A sigh held until the girdle of the loins breaks
A prophet ridiculed for grieving in public

8.pericope_label: A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished: it is sharpened to make a sore slaughter; it is furbished that it may glitter
debates: Whether the rod of my son is the object or the subject of the clause
Whether the sword in view is the Chaldean or the Roman
What the trial of the thirteenth verse means
outliers: Ellicott makes the clause an objection put into the mouth of the hearer, that the promise to Judah is sure whatever power rises against it
Clarke reads the same clause the other way, as the sword despising the power of the people God called his son
Ellicott admits the original is obscure in its extreme brevity and that the versions have changed the text without improvement
Henry answers the fear that the sword will exceed its commission by insisting it is a trial and no more than a trial
themes: A sword rubbed bright after rusting in the scabbard
A passage of Homer on a god smiting his thighs
An axe boasting itself against the one who hews with it
Princes whose dignity is no security

14.pericope_label: Also, thou son of man, appoint thee two ways, that the sword of the king of Babylon may come: both twain shall come forth out of one land
debates: What the word rendered the point of the sword means
Whether the word rendered slain means killed or overthrown
What the doubling of the sword the third time counts
outliers: Ellicott renders the rare word as the glance or the whirl of the sword and the multiplied ruins as multiplied stumbling blocks
Clarke counts three campaigns of the king of Babylon, against Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah, and takes the word for slain as meaning soldier
Ellicott insists the two ways are seen in vision, since the roads from Babylon would run together for many hundred miles
Ellicott corrects choose thou a place to make a hand, a finger-post set up to direct the king on his march
themes: A sword addressed as a host and told to close ranks right and set itself left
A sword kept wrapped so that it might not be blunted
Politics that leave a conqueror at a loss
Gates of cities, palaces and private houses alike

21.pericope_label: For the king of Babylon stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination
debates: Whether the diadem is the royal crown or the priestly mitre
Who calls the iniquity to remembrance, God or the king of Babylon
Whether the liver was read for omens or inspected for soundness
outliers: Ellicott holds that the word rendered diadem is everywhere else the mitre of the high priest, so that the priestly office fell with the royal
Ellicott prefers shook his arrows to made his arrows bright, and calls the rite simply one form of casting lots
Clarke thinks the liver was inspected only to show whether the victim was sound, a diseased animal being a bad omen
Gill takes the threefold overturning for the utter abolition of the kingly power rather than for three generations
themes: Three headless arrows drawn from a bag
A rite of divination outlawed by the Koran
This not this, read as an utter change of the whole existing state
A prophet permitted to call a king wicked

28.pericope_label: And thou, son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord God concerning the Ammonites, and concerning their reproach
debates: Whether the clause about the sheath is a question or a command
Whom the judging in the land of nativity falls upon
How the iniquity of the Ammonites comes to an end
outliers: Ellicott finds nothing in the original to mark a question or the first person, and reads a command to the Ammonites to return the sword into its sheath
Ellicott holds the iniquity ends not through repentance but because it ceases of necessity with the death of the sinner
Clarke refers the judging to the madness that came upon the king of Babylon after his return
Ellicott explains that this prophecy is added lest the heathen infer that the enemies of Israel escape
themes: A nation falling upon the necks of the already slain
Fire turned by the wind upon a forest
Men with the wit of men to do the work of wild beasts
A name blotted out for wishing another name lost
